title: A rocket plane flew so high that eight of its pilots earned astronaut wings

cover.alt: Black-and-white film still: the dark, stubby-winged X-15 rocket plane hangs beneath the wing of a B-52 bomber, high above the ground.

body: The **X-15** never took off on its own. A B-52 carried it up under one wing and dropped it at about 45,000 feet (13.7 km) and 500 mph; then its rocket engine could burn 15,000 lb of propellant in about 80 seconds. Near the top of its climb the air was too thin for wings and fins to work, so the pilot steered with small rocket thrusters. Three X-15s made 199 flights, the last in 1968, and 13 of them, by eight pilots, went above 50 miles, the US Air Force’s boundary of space.

slides.alt: Black-and-white newsreel: the X-15 hangs under the B-52’s wing, drops away trailing smoke, an on-board camera looks back along its tail at rocket trails, a white contrail climbs, then the camera looks down at Earth from high altitude.
slides.caption: Newsreel of Robert White’s climb to 95.9 km, July 1962: the X-15 drops from the B-52 and lights its rocket; on-board cameras look back, then down at Earth.

slides.heading: How high the X-15 went
slides.note: The Air Force line is 50 miles. Only Joe Walker’s two highest flights passed 100 km.

slides.label: Robert White’s speed on his climb to 95.9 km on 17 July 1962
slides.text: By the Air Force’s 50-mile rule it was the X-15’s first spaceflight, and White, an Air Force pilot, got astronaut wings for it.

slides.question: An X-15 flight in 1967 set a record that still stands. Which one?
slides.explanation: On 3 October 1967 Pete Knight reached Mach 6.7, about 4,520 mph (7,274 km/h). It remains the official speed record for a crewed, powered aircraft.

slides.prompt: Three civilian NASA pilots also flew the X-15 past 50 miles, but got no astronaut wings at the time. When did they get them?
slides.detail: NASA awarded them retroactively: to Bill Dana, who was still living, and posthumously to John McKay and Joe Walker.
